title: Neri v. Senate Committee on Accountability
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the claim of executive privilege by NEDA Director General Neri, who refused to answer questions before the Senate regarding communications with President Arroyo about the NBN-ZTE deal. The presidential communications privilege covers advisory opinions given to the President.
doctrine: Executive privilege is constitutionally based and covers presidential communications. The presidential communications privilege applies to documents and communications that reflect the deliberative process of the President. However, this privilege is not absolute and may yield to the need for evidence in a criminal case.
fullText:
LEONARDO-DE CASTRO, J.:

This case involves the power of the Senate to compel the attendance and testimony of executive officials at legislative inquiries.

The presidential communications privilege is fundamental to the operation of government and inextricably rooted in the separation of powers under the Constitution. It applies to documents or other materials that reflect presidential decision-making and deliberations.

The elements of presidential communications privilege are: (1) the protected communication must relate to a quintessential and non-delegable presidential power; (2) the communication must be authored or solicited and received by a close advisor of the President; and (3) the communication must be made in the course of preparing advice for the President.
